pathophysiology.summary: Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) results from arterial occlusion and sudden cerebral hypoperfusion. Reperfusion treatment seeks to preserve potentially salvageable tissue while avoiding haemorrhagic harm.
keyMechanisms: Large-artery atherosclerosis may cause in-situ thrombosis or artery-to-artery embolism.
Cardioembolism includes atrial fibrillation and structural cardiac sources.
Small-vessel disease can cause lacunar infarction; dissection and hypercoagulable disorders are alternative causes.
Earlier reperfusion is associated with greater benefit; eligible patients need urgent specialist imaging and treatment decisions.
Hypoxaemia, hyperglycaemia and fever may worsen acute brain injury and require protocol-directed assessment.

symptoms: Sudden unilateral face, arm or leg weakness or sensory loss.
Aphasia, dysarthria, neglect, gaze deviation or homonymous visual-field loss.
Vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, crossed signs or reduced consciousness can indicate posterior-circulation stroke.
physicalSigns: Record National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score and repeat it if the deficit changes.
Assess pulse rhythm, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, glucose and signs of trauma, seizure or infection.
A severe cortical deficit raises concern for large-vessel occlusion and urgent vascular imaging.
redFlags: Last-known-well time within a reperfusion window or unknown-onset/wake-up stroke: activate the local stroke pathway immediately.
Severe deficit, gaze deviation, aphasia, neglect, dense hemiparesis, coma or fluctuating brainstem signs: urgent stroke-team and thrombectomy-centre discussion.
Anticoagulant exposure, bleeding tendency, severe headache, vomiting, seizure or falling consciousness: urgent brain imaging to assess haemorrhage and other alternatives.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Cannot be safely distinguished from ischaemia clinically; urgent brain imaging is required.
Capillary glucose can identify a reversible mimic during immediate assessment.
A witnessed seizure supports the diagnosis, but seizure at onset does not by itself exclude ischemic stroke.
Symptoms often spread gradually and may be positive; a new focal deficit still needs an urgent stroke assessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Activate the acute stroke pathway
actions: Record last-known-well and discovery times, establish airway, breathing and circulation, and obtain glucose.
Record baseline NIHSS and arrange urgent brain imaging with stroke-team review.
Keep the patient nil by mouth until a validated swallow screen is passed.

clinicalManagement.title: Image and make reperfusion decisions
actions: Use non-contrast CT to assess haemorrhage and urgent vascular imaging when large-vessel occlusion or thrombectomy is suspected.
Offer intravenous thrombolysis only through the current specialist and local-protocol eligibility pathway; the ESO guideline supports alteplase within 4.5 hours for eligible adults.
For wake-up or selected late presentations, use specialist advanced-imaging selection; do not exclude solely because the onset is unknown.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate possible large-vessel occlusion
actions: Discuss confirmed or strongly suspected large-vessel occlusion with the stroke and neurointerventional team immediately.
Do not delay thrombectomy-centre transfer solely to observe response to intravenous thrombolysis when both treatments are indicated by the local pathway.
Use local transfer, imaging and eligibility criteria for anterior and posterior circulation occlusions.

clinicalManagement.title: Provide early stroke-unit supportive care
actions: Monitor neurological status, blood pressure, oxygenation, temperature and glucose using the local stroke protocol.
After intravenous thrombolysis, withhold antithrombotics and obtain follow-up brain imaging according to the local post-thrombolysis protocol before starting them.
If reperfusion is not used, initiate antithrombotic treatment only after haemorrhage is excluded and according to the local stroke protocol.

clinicalManagement.title: Admit, rehabilitate and plan secondary prevention
actions: Admit to an acute stroke unit or transfer to an appropriate specialist centre.
Assess swallowing, mobility, communication, rehabilitation needs and cardioembolic/vascular cause.
Document emergency return precautions, medication plan and stroke-service follow-up before discharge.

teaching.scope: Adult emergency recognition and specialist escalation for acute ischemic stroke; not a substitute for the Saudi hospital stroke protocol.
learningObjectives: Recognise possible AIS and important mimics.
Prioritise time-critical imaging and reperfusion referral.
Apply swallowing and post-reperfusion safety checks.
pitfalls: Using a normal early CT to exclude ischemic stroke.
Treating a possible large-vessel occlusion without early vascular imaging and specialist discussion.
Copying drug doses or exclusions without confirming the current local protocol and authorised product.
keyPoints: Record last-known-well time and activate the stroke pathway immediately.
Brain imaging is required to assess haemorrhage before ischemic reperfusion treatment.
Advanced imaging can support selected wake-up and late-window decisions.
Do not give oral medicines, food or fluid before a swallow screen.
